results.title: Incident documentation
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines the information that should be tracked, documented, and reported for serious incidents, including root cause analysis, mitigation failures or circumvention, and handling of incomplete information.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework specify the minimum information set for serious incident documentation and reporting, including root cause analysis and treatment of missing information?
expected_evidence: The framework defines the categories of information to be documented for serious incidents (e.g. timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, and response actions).
The framework specifies that a root cause analysis should be conducted, including examination of model outputs, inputs, and any failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations.
The framework describes how patterns or signals from post-market monitoring may inform incident analysis.
The framework acknowledges that some information may be unavailable at the time of reporting and requires such gaps to be explicitly recorded.
The framework indicates that the level of detail in serious incident documentation should be proportionate to the severity of the incident.
results.reasoning: No indicators are clearly met: the text cites incident tracking/monitoring and communication, but fails to specify a minimum information set, root cause analysis, handling of missing information, use of post-market signals for incident analysis, or proportional detail tied to severity. These gaps cannot be offset by thematic alignment alone.
key_aligned_concepts: Incident documentation and tracking
Post-deployment monitoring and incident response
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Minimum information set for serious incidents (timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, and response actions)
Requirement to conduct root cause analysis (including examination of model outputs, inputs, and any failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations)
Explicit handling of incomplete/missing information (explicitly recording gaps at time of reporting)
Defined method for using post-market monitoring signals to inform incident analysis
Explicit coverage of mitigation failures or circumvention within incident documentation

results.title: Reporting timelines
results.requirement: The framework defines mandatory severity-based reporting timelines for serious incidents involving the model, including differentiated deadlines for initial reports based on incident type, requirements for periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and submission of a final report after incident resolution.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework specify clearly differentiated reporting timelines for serious incidents (including specific deadlines for initial notification based on severity), periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and a final report after resolution?
expected_evidence: The framework defines categories of serious incidents (e.g., critical infrastructure disruption, cybersecurity breach, death, serious harm to health, fundamental rights, property or environment).
The framework associates specific deadlines for initial reporting following awareness of a serious incident (e.g., two days, five days, ten days, fifteen days depending on severity).
The framework clarifies that reporting is triggered when the organisation becomes aware of the involvement of its model, including cases of reasonable suspicion of causal linkage.
The framework specifies periodic intermediate updates for unresolved serious incidents (e.g., at least every four weeks after the initial report).
The framework defines a deadline for submitting a final report after resolution of the serious incident (e.g., within 60 days after resolution).

1.2.3
Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

results.requirement: Define and maintain retention requirements ensuring that serious-incident documentation is preserved for at least five years from the later of the documentation date or the incident date.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define retention requirements for serious-incident documentation that meet or exceed a five-year period?
expected_evidence: The framework states that documentation of information related to serious incidents must be retained.
The framework specifies a minimum retention period of at least five years.
The framework indicates that the retention period is counted from the later of the documentation date or the date of the serious incident.
results.reasoning: No indicators of retention for serious-incident documentation are present: the retrieved text lacks (1) a requirement that such documentation be retained, (2) a five-year minimum retention period, and (3) the rule that the retention period is counted from the later of the documentation date or incident date. Given these are binary operational requirements, absence cannot be offset by thematic alignment to governance or version-control content.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: The framework lacks retention requirements for serious-incident documentation and does not specify a five-year minimum or the calculation method for the retention period.

The framework should also define how key systemic risk decisions and justifications are documented.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define requirements to maintain, retain, and make available additional detailed documentation and decision justifications for AI Office review?

Documentation defines requirements for describing model integration into AI systems (where applicable).
Documentation defines requirements for documenting model evaluations, results, and evaluation strategies.
Documentation defines requirements for documenting implemented safety mitigations.
Documentation defines how key systemic risk processes, decisions, and justifications are recorded.
Documentation specifies retention periods for additional documentation (e.g. at least 10 years).

It is missing explicit content requirements for architecture, integration, evaluations and results, safety mitigations, and the retention/delivery obligations (10-year retention and AI Office access). results.title: Public transparency
results.requirement: Define when and how summarised public versions of the Framework and Model Reports are published for the purpose of systemic risk assessment and mitigation, including safeguards to protect sensitive information and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations. The framework should also define conditions under which public publication is not required (e.g. similarly safe or safer models).
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define conditions, scope, safeguards, and exceptions for publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports?
expected_evidence: The framework states that summarised versions of the Framework and Model Reports may be published.
The framework indicates that publication is required when necessary for systemic risk assessment or mitigation.
The framework indicates that removals or redactions are applied to protect sensitive commercial information and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations.
The framework states that Model Report summaries include high-level descriptions of systemic risk assessment results and safety and security mitigations.
The framework defines exceptions where publication is not required for similarly safe or safer models.
results.reasoning: The retrieved text provides no explicit indicators for publishing public summaries of the Framework or Model Reports, no publication triggers, scope, safeguards, or exceptions. Consequently, none of the five expected indicators are present, and thematic alignment on transparency does not substitute for the required operational publication provisions.
key_aligned_concepts: Transparency and accountability as governing principles in AI RMF
GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE core functions
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Missing explicit publication conditions or triggers for public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports.
Missing defined publication scope and target audience for summaries.
Missing safeguards for public summaries (e.g., redaction or aggregation) to protect sensitive information and maintain effectiveness of mitigations.
Missing requirement to include high-level descriptions of systemic risk assessment results and safety/security mitigations in Model Report summaries.
Missing defined exceptions where publication is not required for similarly safe or safer models.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: No, the retrieved AI RMF text does not define conditions, scope, safeguards, or exceptions for publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text emphasizes transparency as a governance principle and outlines core risk-management functions, but it does not specify public publication of Framework or Model Reports or any redaction/safeguard mechanisms, so it does not meet the specific SS-10.2 requirement.
key_aligned_concepts: Transparency and accountability as governing principles in AI RMF

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The retrieved AI RMF text does not specify any conditions, scope, safeguards, or exceptions for publishing public summaries of the Framework or Model Reports, nor does it mention redaction/removal of sensitive information or when publication is required or not required.
missing_elements: Explicit conditions or triggers for publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports.
Defined publication scope (whether summaries pertain to the Framework, Model Reports, or both) and target audience.
Safeguards for public summaries (e.g., redaction, aggregation) to protect sensitive commercial information and preserve effectiveness of safety and security mitigations.

Defined exceptions where publication is not required for similarly safe or safer models.

criteria.title: Implement the Safety & Security Framework
criteria.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework is intended to be applied across the entire model lifecycle, including continuous systemic risk assessment activities, trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident inputs, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how its systemic risk assessment and mitigation processes are intended to be applied across the model lifecycle, including continuous assessment activities, trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident consideration, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment?
expected_evidence: The framework describes how systemic risks are continuously assessed along the entire model lifecycle.
The framework explains how lighter-touch evaluations are conducted at predefined trigger points (e.g. based on time, development stage, compute, access, or affordances).
The framework describes how post-market monitoring is conducted to inform ongoing systemic risk assessment.
The framework explains how information about serious incidents or near misses is taken into account within the risk assessment process.

The framework describes how results from trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, or incident inputs can lead to deeper analysis or escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process.
The framework outlines the sequence or structure of the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (identification, analysis, acceptability determination, mitigation, and re-assessment).
criteria.reasoning: Found indicators: continuous lifecycle monitoring (E1_ContinuousLifecycleAssessment), post-market monitoring (E3_PostMarketMonitoring), incident inputs (E4_IncidentInputs), and lifecycle applicability (E1_LifecycleApplicability). Missing: explicit trigger-point evaluations, a formal escalation pathway from trigger points/post-market/incidents to a full systemic risk assessment and a defined end-to-end SRA sequence (identification, analysis, acceptability, mitigation, re-assessment). These gaps prevent full compliance; thematic alignment cannot compensate for missing operational mechanisms.

lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set of actors (See

visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts. The interdependencies

anticipate impacts of AI systems. For example, early decisions in identifying purposes and
objectives of an AI system can alter its behavior and capabilities, and the dynamics of deployment setting (such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI

can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.

criteria.title: Framework updates
criteria.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework defines the conditions, processes, and scope for periodic and event-driven framework assessments and updates, including versioning, changelogs, and remediation planning, in line with Measure 1.3 of the Safety and Security Chapter.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define how and when framework assessments and updates are intended to occur, including assessment triggers, periodic review, evaluation of framework adequacy and adherence, and the handling of remediation and versioning?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that it is subject to periodic reassessment (e.g. at defined intervals) and to reassessment when specified conditions or events occur.

The framework describes conditions or triggers that would lead to a framework assessment (e.g. material changes in model development, serious incidents or near misses, materially changed systemic risks or model capabilities).
The framework explains the scope of a framework assessment, including the evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to the systemic risks of the models.
The framework explains that framework adherence is assessed, including consideration of non-adherence and its causes.
The framework describes how findings from a framework assessment may lead to updates of the framework to keep it state-of-the-art.
The framework describes that updates are intended to be versioned and accompanied by a changelog explaining the nature and rationale of changes.
The framework describes how remediation plans are intended to be defined when framework assessments identify risks of continued or future non-adherence.
criteria.reasoning: The text presents versioning with a changelog, and a living-document approach with semi-annual updates, satisfying indicators on versioning, changelog, and periodic review. However, it fails to specify explicit assessment triggers, periodic reassessment cadence, evaluation of framework adequacy/adherence, and remediation planning, leaving several structural indicators unmet.
key_aligned_concepts: Versioning and changelog tracking
Living document / update process
Periodic review of updates
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit assessment triggers or events that initiate a framework assessment are not defined.
No defined periodic reassessment cadence for the framework.
No defined scope of a framework assessment (assessing adequacy against systemic risks).
No explicit process for assessing framework adherence or identifying causes of non-adherence.
No mechanism showing how assessment findings lead to updates to keep the framework state-of-the-art, and no remediation planning procedures.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Partially; the text defines a versioning system with a changelog and ongoing updates (living document) but does not specify explicit assessment triggers, periodic framework reassessments, evaluation of adequacy/adherence, or remediation planning processes.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework demonstrates alignment on versioning, change tracking, and ongoing updates; it does not provide explicit triggers, periodic reassessment cadence, or remediation planning as required.
key_aligned_concepts: Versioning and changelog tracking
Living document / update process

criteria.requirement: Acknowledge the obligation to notify the AI Office of the Safety and Security Framework and its updates, in line with Measure 1.4 of the Safety and Security Chapter.

expected_evidence: The framework explicitly acknowledges an obligation to notify or inform the AI Office about the Safety and Security Framework.

conjunction with the AI community.

whether the AI RMF has improved their ability to manage AI risks, including but not limited to their policies, processes, practices, implementation plans, indicators, measurements,
and expected outcomes. NIST intends to work collaboratively with others to develop metrics, methodologies, and goals for evaluating the AI RMF’s effectiveness, and to broadly
share results and supporting information. Framework users are expected to benefit from:
• enhanced processes for governing, mapping, measuring, and managing AI risk, and
clearly documenting outcomes;

• enhanced organizational culture which prioritizes the identification and management
of AI system risks and potential impacts to individuals, communities, organizations,
and society;

continue to develop, and to be operationalized by organizations in varying degrees and

criteria.title: Risk identification process
criteria.requirement: Define a structured systemic risk identification process that is explicitly informed by the types of risks, the nature of systemic risks, and the sources of systemic risks as set out in Appendix 1, and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define a structured systemic risk identification process that is informed by the risk types (Appendix 1.1), the nature of systemic risks (Appendix 1.2), the sources of systemic risks (Appendix 1.3), and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks (Appendix 1.4)?
expected_evidence: The framework describes a structured process for identifying systemic risks stemming from the model.

The framework indicates that potential systemic risks are initially considered with reference to the types of risks defined in Appendix 1.1 (e.g. risks to public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, and society).

The framework explains that the identification process considers the nature of systemic risks, including essential and contributing characteristics such as scale, propagation, capability-dependence, or irreversibility (Appendix 1.2).

The framework describes how potential sources of systemic risks are considered in the identification process, including model capabilities, model propensities, and model affordances or contextual factors (Appendix 1.3).

The framework explicitly indicates that the specified systemic risks listed in Appendix 1.4 are taken into account as part of the systemic risk identification process, such as risks related to chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) threats, loss of control of the model, large-scale cyber offence, and harmful manipulation.
criteria.reasoning: No indicators are evidenced. criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the gathering of model-independent information relevant to systemic risk analysis, including how the breadth and depth of information gathering are determined in relation to the systemic risk.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the organisation systematically gather and document model-independent information relevant to identified systemic risks, using structured methods such as web searches or OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses of comparable models, training data reviews, historical incident analysis, forecasting of technological trends, expert consultations, and/or stakeholder or community engagement?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that systemic risk analysis is informed by model-independent information.
The framework explains that the breadth and depth of model-independent information gathering are adjusted based on the characteristics or severity of the systemic risk.

The framework indicates categories of methods that may be used to gather model-independent information, such as web searches or open-source intelligence, literature reviews, market analyses, reviews of historical incident data, forecasting of general trends, expert interviews or panels, and participatory or community-based research methods.

The framework clarifies the role of model-independent information in informing subsequent stages of systemic risk analysis (e.g. evaluations, modelling, or estimation), without requiring that such stages have already been performed.
criteria.reasoning: Indicator A is met (framework indicates systemic risk analysis is informed by model-independent external information). Indicators B and C are not demonstrated (no explicit breadth/depth adjustment rules or enumerated methods). Indicator D is not clearly evidenced as a defined linkage to downstream analytical stages. Therefore, partial compliance is identified.
key_aligned_concepts: External, model-independent information informs systemic risk management practices.
Structured engagement with external AI actors and documented contextual information collection.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Absence of explicit enumeration of model-independent information-gathering methods (e.g., OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses, training data reviews, historical incident analyses, forecasting of technological trends, expert consultations, stakeholder/community engagement).
No defined rule describing how the breadth and depth of information gathering scale with the characteristics or severity of the systemic risk.
No explicit description of how model-independent information feeds subsequent risk-analysis steps (evaluations, modelling, estimation) with traceability.

Effectiveness of the AI RMF
Evaluations of AI RMF effectiveness – including ways to measure bottom-line improvements in the trustworthiness of AI systems – will be part of future NIST activities, in

whether the AI RMF has improved their ability to manage AI risks, including but not limited to their policies, processes, practices, implementation plans, indicators, measurements,

of AI system risks and potential impacts to individuals, communities, organizations,

criteria.title: Risk estimation
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the estimation of the probability and severity of harm for systemic risks, using at least state-of-the-art risk estimation methods and taking into account relevant information inputs.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how the probability and severity of harm for systemic risks are intended to be estimated using state-of-the-art methods, taking into account relevant information from systemic risk identification, analysis, and serious incident reporting, and how such estimates are expressed?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that probability and severity of harm are estimated as part of systemic risk analysis.
The framework indicates that at least state-of-the-art risk estimation methods are used, appropriate to the systemic risk being assessed.

The framework explains that risk estimation takes into account relevant information inputs, such as outputs from systemic risk identification and analysis and information about serious incidents or near misses.

The framework describes how estimates of systemic risk are expressed, for example as risk scores, risk matrices, probability distributions, or other qualitative, semi-quantitative, or quantitative formats.
The framework explains the purpose of risk estimation in supporting systemic risk acceptance determination, without requiring specific numerical or qualitative results.
criteria.reasoning: None of the five expected indicators are evidenced: there is no operational description of estimating systemic-risk probability/severity with state-of-the-art methods, no use of inputs from systemic risk identification or incident reporting, no explicit formats for expressing systemic-risk estimates, and no stated purpose for risk estimation in risk acceptance decisions. The text only provides a high-level definition of risk (probability × consequence) without operational systemic-risk estimation mechanics.

criteria.title: Post-market monitoring
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines post-market monitoring to gather information relevant to systemic risk assessment and updating, and how independent external evaluators are intended to be enabled under appropriate safeguards, where applicable.
criteria.assessment_question: What post-market monitoring methods are required for assessing and mitigating systemic risk, and under what conditions and safeguards must independent external evaluators be granted access to model versions, chains-of-thought, and safety-reduced model variants, including protections against legal retaliation and responsible vulnerability disclosure timelines?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that post-market monitoring is conducted to gather information about the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects.
The framework explains that post-market monitoring informs systemic risk acceptability determinations and decisions on framework or report updates.

The framework indicates that a range of post-market monitoring methods may be used, such as collecting end-user feedback, providing reporting or incident channels, engaging with affected stakeholders, monitoring public sources, or supporting independent research.
The framework describes how post-market monitoring applies when the model is integrated into AI systems provided or deployed by the Signatory.
The framework describes whether and under what conditions independent external evaluators are intended to be provided with access to the model for post-market monitoring purposes.

The framework explains the safeguards associated with external evaluator access, such as selection criteria, information security measures, responsible disclosure procedures, and non-retaliation commitments.
criteria.reasoning: Two indicators are evidenced (in-production post-market monitoring; safeguards for external evaluator access), but four indicators are missing: explicit access conditions to model versions/chains-of-thought/safety-reduced variants, timelines for vulnerability disclosure, detailed enumerated post-market monitoring methods for Signatory deployments, and clear applicability/governance for Signatory deployments. Thematic alignment cannot compensate for these operational, binary requirements.
key_aligned_concepts: In-production monitoring (TEVV) to support risk management
Safeguards for external evaluator access (selection criteria, information security, responsible disclosure, non-retaliation)
Measurement outcomes informing risk monitoring and response
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit, binding access conditions for independent external evaluators to model versions, chain-of-thought logs, and safety-reduced variants (including retention, auditing, scope, time-bound access)
Explicit timelines for responsible vulnerability disclosure by providers/owners

Detailed, enumerated post-market monitoring methods (end-user feedback channels, incident reporting channels, stakeholder engagement processes, monitoring public sources, support for independent research) for Signatory deployments
Clear applicability to AI systems provided or deployed by the Signatory, including deployment-specific monitoring obligations and governance

Operational safeguards for external evaluators beyond general statements (refined selection criteria, data handling/minimization, independent audit rights, conflict-of-interest safeguards, remedy procedures)

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The text discusses in-production post-market monitoring and external evaluator safeguards in general, and specifies safeguards for external evaluator access, but does not provide detailed conditions for access to model versions, chains-of-thought, or safety-reduced variants, nor explicit timelines.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework establishes in-production monitoring and links measurement outcomes to risk management, and it explicitly lists safeguards for external evaluator access; however, it stops short of detailing access conditions for specific model variants and lacks explicit timelines.

criteria.title: Acceptance criteria
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines and justifies systemic risk acceptance criteria or tiers for each identified systemic risk, including how acceptability is determined at the individual and overall level and how safety margins are incorporated.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework describe and justify how systemic risk acceptance criteria or tiers are defined for each identified systemic risk, how they are used to determine acceptability at the individual and overall level, and how appropriate safety margins are incorporated?
expected_evidence: The framework describes how systemic risk acceptance is determined for each identified systemic risk.
The framework defines systemic risk acceptance tiers or, where tiers are not suitable and the risk is not a specified systemic risk, alternative acceptance criteria.

The framework explains that acceptance tiers or criteria are measurable and are defined primarily in terms of model capabilities, and may also incorporate model propensities, risk estimates, or other suitable metrics.
The framework indicates that at least one systemic risk tier exists that has not yet been reached by the model.
The framework describes how acceptance criteria or tiers are used to determine acceptability for each systemic risk and for the overall systemic risk.

The framework explains how safety margins are incorporated into acceptance determination, taking into account uncertainty, potential future changes in model capabilities or usage, limitations of risk assessments, and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations.

The Framework is intended to be flexible and to augment existing risk practices

1.2.3
Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

All involved AI actors share responsibilities for designing, developing, and deploying a
trustworthy AI system that is fit for purpose.
Risk in real-world settings: While measuring AI risks in a laboratory or a controlled
environment may yield important insights pre-deployment, these measurements may differ
from risks that emerge in operational, real-world settings.
Inscrutability: Inscrutable AI systems can complicate risk measurement. Inscrutability
can be a result of the opaque nature of AI systems (limited explainability or interpretability), lack of transparency or documentation in AI system development or deployment, or
inherent uncertainties in AI systems.
Human baseline: Risk management of AI systems that are intended to augment or replace
human activity, for example decision making, requires some form of baseline metrics for
comparison. This is difficult to systematize since AI systems carry out different tasks – and
perform tasks differently – than humans.

is acceptable to organizations or society are highly contextual and application and use-case

roles and responsibilities, culture, and incentive structures for risk management to be effective. Use of the AI RMF alone will not lead to these changes or provide the appropriate
incentives. Effective risk management is realized through organizational commitment at
senior levels and may require cultural change within an organization or industry. In addition, small to medium-sized organizations managing AI risks or implementing the AI RMF
may face different challenges than large organizations, depending on their capabilities and
resources.

NIST AI 100-1
AI RMF 1.0
Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,
such as threats to civil liberties and rights, while also providing opportunities to maximize
positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.
1.1
Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the
negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of
occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.
“Risk management refers to coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk” (Source: ISO 31000:2018).

Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

criteria.requirement: The framework defines and requires the implementation of safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle that are appropriate to identified systemic risks, sufficiently robust under adversarial pressure, and taking into account the model’s release and distribution strategy, with the objective of ensuring that systemic risks are acceptable
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define and require the implementation of safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle that are appropriate to identified systemic risks, sufficiently robust under adversarial pressure, and taking into account the model’s release and distribution strategy, with the objective of ensuring that systemic risks are acceptable?
expected_evidence: The framework describes categories or types of safety mitigations intended to address systemic risks.
The framework explains that safety mitigations are designed to be robust under adversarial pressure, such as attempts to bypass or subvert them.
The framework indicates that safety mitigations take into account the model's release and distribution strategy.
The framework provides examples of safety mitigation approaches, such as e.g. input or output filtering, behaviour modification, staged access, or other emerging safety techniques.
The framework indicates that safety mitigations are considered and adapted across the model lifecycle.
criteria.reasoning: Indicators 1, 3, 4, and 5 are supported by the text (categories/examples of mitigations, release/deployment considerations, lifecycle-adaptive mitigations). Robustness or generalizability is defined as the “ability of a system to maintain its level
of performance under a variety of circumstances” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Robustness is a goal for appropriate system functionality in a broad set of conditions and
circumstances, including uses of AI systems not initially anticipated. Robustness requires
not only that the system perform exactly as it does under expected uses, but also that it
should perform in ways that minimize potential harms to people if it is operating in an
unexpected setting.
Validity and reliability for deployed AI systems are often assessed by ongoing testing or
monitoring that confirms a system is performing as intended. Measurement of validity,
accuracy, robustness, and reliability contribute to trustworthiness and should take into consideration that certain types of failures can cause greater harm. AI risk management efforts
should prioritize the minimization of potential negative impacts, and may need to include
human intervention in cases where the AI system cannot detect or correct errors.
3.2
Safe
AI systems should “not under defined conditions, lead to a state in which human life,
health, property, or the environment is endangered” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Safe
operation of AI systems is improved through:
• responsible design, development, and deployment practices;
• clear information to deployers on responsible use of the system;

safety in fields such as transportation and healthcare, and align with existing sector- or
application-specific guidelines or standards.
3.3
Secure and Resilient
AI systems, as well as the ecosystems in which they are deployed, may be said to be resilient if they can withstand unexpected adverse events or unexpected changes in their environment or use – or if they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of internal
and external change and degrade safely and gracefully when this is necessary (Adapted
from: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Common security concerns relate to adversarial examples,
data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property
through AI system endpoints. AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and
availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may
be said to be secure. Guidelines in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and Risk Management Framework are among those which are applicable here.
Security and resilience are related but distinct characteristics. While resilience is the ability to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event, security includes resilience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover
from attacks. Resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data
to encompass unexpected or adversarial use (or abuse or misuse) of the model or data.

Robustness or generalizability is defined as the “ability of a system to maintain its level
of performance under a variety of circumstances” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Robustness is a goal for appropriate system functionality in a broad set of conditions and
circumstances, including uses of AI systems not initially anticipated. Robustness requires
not only that the system perform exactly as it does under expected uses, but also that it
should perform in ways that minimize potential harms to people if it is operating in an
unexpected setting.
Validity and reliability for deployed AI systems are often assessed by ongoing testing or
monitoring that confirms a system is performing as intended. Measurement of validity,
accuracy, robustness, and reliability contribute to trustworthiness and should take into consideration that certain types of failures can cause greater harm. AI risk management efforts
should prioritize the minimization of potential negative impacts, and may need to include
human intervention in cases where the AI system cannot detect or correct errors.
3.2
Safe
AI systems should “not under defined conditions, lead to a state in which human life,
health, property, or the environment is endangered” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Safe
operation of AI systems is improved through:
• responsible design, development, and deployment practices;

safety in fields such as transportation and healthcare, and align with existing sector- or
application-specific guidelines or standards.
3.3
Secure and Resilient
AI systems, as well as the ecosystems in which they are deployed, may be said to be resilient if they can withstand unexpected adverse events or unexpected changes in their environment or use – or if they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of internal
and external change and degrade safely and gracefully when this is necessary (Adapted
from: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Common security concerns relate to adversarial examples,
data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property
through AI system endpoints. AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and
availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may
be said to be secure. Guidelines in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and Risk Management Framework are among those which are applicable here.
Security and resilience are related but distinct characteristics. While resilience is the ability to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event, security includes resilience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover
from attacks. Resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data
to encompass unexpected or adversarial use (or abuse or misuse) of the model or data.

frameworks based on the domain addressed – and because AI risk management calls for

At the same time, guidance available before publication of this AI RMF does not comprehensively address many AI system risks. For example, existing frameworks and guidance

evidence.text:
Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

the effectiveness of testing and can mitigate internal biases and potential conflicts of interest.
Where tradeoffs among the trustworthy characteristics arise, measurement provides a traceable basis to inform management decisions. Options may include recalibration, impact
mitigation, or removal of the system from design, development, production, or use, as well
as a range of compensating, detective, deterrent, directive, and recovery controls.
After completing the MEASURE function, objective, repeatable, or scalable test, evaluation,
verification, and validation (TEVV) processes including metrics, methods, and methodologies are in place, followed, and documented. Metrics and measurement methodologies
should adhere to scientific, legal, and ethical norms and be carried out in an open and transparent process. New types of measurement, qualitative and quantitative, may need to be
developed. The degree to which each measurement type provides unique and meaningful
information to the assessment of AI risks should be considered. Framework users will enhance their capacity to comprehensively evaluate system trustworthiness, identify and track
existing and emergent risks, and verify efficacy of the metrics. Measurement outcomes will
be utilized in the MANAGE function to assist risk monitoring and response efforts. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue applying the MEASURE function to AI systems
as knowledge, methodologies, risks, and impacts evolve over time.

The Model Report describes how the model has been used and how it is intended to be used, including relevant use contexts.
The Model Report identifies model versions that are or will be made available on the market and explains relevant differences, including differences in systemic risks or mitigations.

The Model Report includes or references a model specification describing how the model is intended to operate, including guiding principles, prioritisation of instructions, refusal topics, and the system prompt (or a valid reference to it).

1.2.3
Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

Description of scaling effects or scaling laws indicating novel or materially enhanced model capabilities
Summarisation of novel model architectures that materially improve computational efficiency or capabilities

Description of training techniques that materially improve the efficiency or feasibility of training (e.g., distributed or large-scale training)

scope_divergences: Divergence between external regulatory framing (EU SS-7.5 requiring Model Reports on systemic-risk landscape changes) and the internal AI RMF-focused governance content provided, which lacks systemic-risk market impact focus

synthesis_result.justification: No indicators from the Expected Evidence are present in the text: it does not describe material changes to the systemic risk landscape, scaling effects, novel architectures affecting efficiency, mitigation-effectiveness information, or training techniques. Risk at different stages of the AI lifecycle: Measuring risk at an earlier stage in the AI
lifecycle may yield different results than measuring risk at a later stage; some risks may
be latent at a given point in time and may increase as AI systems adapt and evolve. Furthermore, different AI actors across the AI lifecycle can have different risk perspectives.
For example, an AI developer who makes AI software available, such as pre-trained models, can have a different risk perspective than an AI actor who is responsible for deploying
that pre-trained model in a specific use case. Such deployers may not recognize that their
particular uses could entail risks which differ from those perceived by the initial developer.
All involved AI actors share responsibilities for designing, developing, and deploying a
trustworthy AI system that is fit for purpose.

resources.

criteria.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines obligations to update the Model Report when the justification for systemic risk acceptability is materially undermined, and whether it specifies periodic update expectations, versioning, and changelog requirements in line with Measure 7.6.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework acknowledge and describe when Model Report updates are required, including material undermining triggers, timing expectations, periodic updates for most capable models, and versioning/changelog requirements?
expected_evidence: The framework describes circumstances under which the justification for systemic risk acceptability may be materially undermined and requires a Model Report update in such cases.
The framework lists or references example triggers for updates, such as material changes in model capabilities, use, integrations, serious incidents, or evaluation validity.
The framework specifies expectations regarding the timing of Model Report updates, including completion within a reasonable time and prior to market release for deliberate changes.
The framework acknowledges periodic Model Report updates for the most capable models (e.g. at least every six months), including applicable exemptions.
The framework requires updated Model Reports to include versioning information and a changelog explaining how and why updates were made.
criteria.reasoning: None of the five Expected Evidence indicators are present in the retrieved text. The text only references versioning (two-number system with a Version Control Table) and a living-document, semi-annual update approach for the AI RMF Playbook, but provides no Model Report update obligations, triggers for material undermining of systemic risk acceptability, timing requirements, six-month cadence for Model Reports, or explicit versioning/changelog requirements for Model Reports.

may consider leveraging available standards and guidance that provide broad guidance to
organizations to reduce security and privacy risks, such as, but not limited to, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the NIST Privacy Framework, the NIST Risk Management Framework, and the Secure Software Development Framework. These frameworks have some
features in common with the AI RMF. Like most risk management approaches, they are
outcome-based rather than prescriptive and are often structured around a Core set of functions, categories, and subcategories. While there are significant differences between these
frameworks based on the domain addressed – and because AI risk management calls for
addressing many other types of risks – frameworks like those mentioned above may inform
security and privacy considerations in the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions of the
AI RMF.
At the same time, guidance available before publication of this AI RMF does not comprehensively address many AI system risks. For example, existing frameworks and guidance
are unable to:
• adequately manage the problem of harmful bias in AI systems;
• confront the challenging risks related to generative AI;
• comprehensively address security concerns related to evasion, model extraction, membership inference, availability, or other machine learning attacks;
• account for the complex attack surface of AI systems or other security abuses enabled
by AI systems; and

Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

criteria.title: AI Office notification
criteria.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework acknowledges the obligation to provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report and any updates, including timing requirements, permitted delays, interim reporting, and conditions for redactions in line with Measure 7.7.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework acknowledge and describe obligations to provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report and updates, including timing rules, permitted delays with interim reporting, and conditions for redactions?
expected_evidence: The framework states that the AI Office must be provided with access to the Model Report by the time a model is placed on the market.
The framework specifies that updates to the Model Report must be made accessible to the AI Office within a defined timeframe (e.g. five business days).
The framework acknowledges conditions under which redactions may be applied, such as requirements arising from national security laws.
The framework describes the possibility of delaying provision of the Model Report or updates for a limited period (e.g. up to 15 business days), subject to good-faith conditions.
The framework requires or acknowledges the provision of an interim Model Report containing specified information when such a delay is used.
The framework describes acceptable access mechanisms (e.g. publicly accessible link or secure channel specified by the AI Office).
criteria.reasoning: None of the six Expected Evidence indicators are present in the retrieved text. The missing indicators include: (1) access by market time for the Model Report; (2) a defined timeframe for updates (e.g., five business days); (3) acknowledgment of redaction conditions; (4) allowance for limited delays under good-faith conditions; (5) provision of an interim Model Report when a delay is used; (6) acceptable access mechanisms (e.g., public link or secure channel). Thematic alignment cannot substitute these concrete operational requirements.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Missing explicit obligations and mechanisms for AI Office access to the Model Report and updates, including timing, delays, interim reporting, redactions, and access methods.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Based on the retrieved text, the framework does not acknowledge or describe obligations to provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report and updates, including timing rules, permitted delays, interim reporting, or redaction conditions.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: There is no evident alignment with the EU Code of Practice requirement on AI Office access to Model Reports; the text focuses on general risk management governance rather than the specified access obligations.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The external framework does not include explicit obligations or mechanisms to provide the AI Office access to the Model Report and updates, nor any timing rules, permitted delays with interim reporting, or redaction conditions. It lacks defined access mechanisms and interim reporting provisions related to delays.
missing_elements: Obligation that the AI Office must be provided access to the Model Report by the time the model is placed on the market.
Definition of a timeframe for updates to the Model Report to be accessible to the AI Office (e.g., a defined number of business days).
Acknowledgement of conditions under which redactions may be applied (e.g., requirements arising from national security or other laws).
Allowance for delaying the provision of the Model Report or updates for a limited period (e.g., up to a specified number of business days) under good-faith conditions.
Requirement or provision of an interim Model Report containing specified information when such a delay is used.
Description of acceptable access mechanisms (e.g., publicly accessible link or a secure channel specified by the AI Office).

Thematic alignment cannot substitute these concrete operational requirements.

As directed by the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 (P.L. 116-283),
the goal of the AI RMF is to offer a resource to the organizations designing, developing,
deploying, or using AI systems to help manage the many risks of AI and promote trustworthy and responsible development and use of AI systems. The Framework is intended to be
voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector-specific, and use-case agnostic, providing flexibility to organizations of all sizes and in all sectors and throughout society to implement the
approaches in the Framework.
The Framework is designed to equip organizations and individuals – referred to here as
AI actors – with approaches that increase the trustworthiness of AI systems, and to help
foster the responsible design, development, deployment, and use of AI systems over time.
AI actors are defined by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
(OECD) as “those who play an active role in the AI system lifecycle, including organizations and individuals that deploy or operate AI” [OECD (2019) Artificial Intelligence in
Society—OECD iLibrary] (See Appendix A).
The AI RMF is intended to be practical, to adapt to the AI landscape as AI technologies
continue to develop, and to be operationalized by organizations in varying degrees and
capacities so society can benefit from AI while also being protected from its potential
harms.

criteria.title: Responsibilities
criteria.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines clear responsibilities for managing systemic risks, including systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance, and how these responsibilities are allocated across organisational governance levels.
criteria.assessment_question: How must signatories assign systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance responsibilities across the management body in its supervisory and executive functions, operational teams, and internal and external assurance providers, including role-specific requirements such as separation from core business activities and cascading responsibility structures for SMEs and SMCs?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly defines responsibilities for systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance.
The framework describes how systemic risk oversight is assigned to a supervisory or otherwise independent governance function.
The framework describes how systemic risk ownership is assigned to executive-level functions responsible for risk-producing activities.
The framework describes how systemic risk support and monitoring is assigned to functions that are organisationally independent from core business activities.
The framework describes how systemic risk assurance is provided to a supervisory or independent body, including internal and, where applicable, external assurance.
The framework acknowledges proportional allocation of responsibilities based on organisational size and complexity (e.g. SMEs or SMCs).
criteria.reasoning: Indicator 3 (executive ownership) is fully evidenced and Indicator 1 is partially evidenced (definitions of risk responsibilities exist), while Indicators 2, 4, 5, and 6 require explicit independent supervisory/assurance structures and SME/SMC cascading which are not present; therefore the framework is not fully compliant.
key_aligned_concepts: Executive leadership responsibility for AI risk decisions (GOVERN 2.3)
Documented roles and lines of communication for AI risk management (GOVERN 2.1)
Ongoing monitoring and periodic review of the risk management process (GOVERN 1.5)
GOVERN is a cross-cutting governance function spanning risk management
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No explicit independent supervisory governance function for systemic risk oversight.
No explicit systemic risk support and monitoring by functions independent from core business activities.
No explicit internal/external assurance mechanism tied to an independent supervisory layer.
No explicit proportional allocation of systemic risk responsibilities for SMEs/SMCs with cascading responsibility structures.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Partially; the text defines executive ownership and documented governance roles for AI risk management across organizational levels and includes ongoing monitoring, but it does not explicitly specify independent supervisory/assurance structures or SME/SMC cascading of responsibilities as required.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The external framework demonstrates governance-level assignment of accountability and explicit executive responsibility for risk decisions, along with documented roles and ongoing monitoring. It does not clearly articulate independent supervisory functions, internal/external assurance, or SME/SMC-specific cascading of risk responsibilities.

Strong governance can drive and enhance internal practices and norms to facilitate organizational risk culture. Governing authorities can determine the overarching policies that
direct an organization’s mission, goals, values, culture, and risk tolerance. Senior leadership sets the tone for risk management within an organization, and with it, organizational
culture. Management aligns the technical aspects of AI risk management to policies and
operations. Documentation can enhance transparency, improve human review processes,
and bolster accountability in AI system teams.
After putting in place the structures, systems, processes, and teams described in the GOVERN function, organizations should benefit from a purpose-driven culture focused on risk

The MANAGE function entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on
a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to
respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events.
Contextual information gleaned from expert consultation and input from relevant AI actors
– established in GOVERN and carried out in MAP – is utilized in this function to decrease
the likelihood of system failures and negative impacts. Systematic documentation practices
established in GOVERN and utilized in MAP and MEASURE bolster AI risk management
efforts and increase transparency and accountability. Processes for assessing emergent risks
are in place, along with mechanisms for continual improvement.
After completing the MANAGE function, plans for prioritizing risk and regular monitoring
and improvement will be in place. Framework users will have enhanced capacity to manage the risks of deployed AI systems and to allocate risk management resources based on
assessed and prioritized risks. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue to apply
the MANAGE function to deployed AI systems as methods, contexts, risks, and needs or
expectations from relevant AI actors evolve over time.

enables the other functions of the process. Aspects of GOVERN, especially those related to

to governance is a continual and intrinsic requirement for effective AI risk management

Strong governance can drive and enhance internal practices and norms to facilitate organizational risk culture. Governing authorities can determine the overarching policies that
direct an organization’s mission, goals, values, culture, and risk tolerance. Senior leadership sets the tone for risk management within an organization, and with it, organizational
culture. Management aligns the technical aspects of AI risk management to policies and
operations. Documentation can enhance transparency, improve human review processes,
and bolster accountability in AI system teams.

criteria.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines methods and channels for identifying and tracking serious incidents across the model lifecycle, including consideration of external sources and facilitation of third-party reporting.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework acknowledge and describe approaches for identifying serious incidents, including monitoring external sources and enabling third-party reporting?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly recognises the need to identify and track serious incidents across the model lifecycle.
The framework describes intended methods for identifying serious incidents, including reference to post-market monitoring or similar processes.
The framework references consideration of external information sources (e.g. media, incident databases, research, public reporting).
The framework describes how downstream providers, users, or other third parties may report serious incidents to the Signatory and/or authorities.
criteria.reasoning: Indicator 1 is addressed (lifecycle-wide monitoring including third-party resources). criteria.title: Incident documentation
criteria.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines the information that should be tracked, documented, and reported for serious incidents, including root cause analysis, mitigation failures or circumvention, and handling of incomplete information.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework specify the minimum information set for serious incident documentation and reporting, including root cause analysis and treatment of missing information?
expected_evidence: The framework defines the categories of information to be documented for serious incidents (e.g. timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, and response actions).
The framework specifies that a root cause analysis should be conducted, including examination of model outputs, inputs, and any failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations.
The framework describes how patterns or signals from post-market monitoring may inform incident analysis.
The framework acknowledges that some information may be unavailable at the time of reporting and requires such gaps to be explicitly recorded.
The framework indicates that the level of detail in serious incident documentation should be proportionate to the severity of the incident.
criteria.reasoning: No indicators are clearly met: the text cites incident tracking/monitoring and communication, but fails to specify a minimum information set, root cause analysis, handling of missing information, use of post-market signals for incident analysis, or proportional detail tied to severity. These gaps cannot be offset by thematic alignment alone.
key_aligned_concepts: Incident documentation and tracking
Post-deployment monitoring and incident response
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Minimum information set for serious incidents (timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, and response actions)
Requirement to conduct root cause analysis (including examination of model outputs, inputs, and any failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations)
Explicit handling of incomplete/missing information (explicitly recording gaps at time of reporting)
Defined method for using post-market monitoring signals to inform incident analysis
Explicit coverage of mitigation failures or circumvention within incident documentation

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: No; the text references incident tracking, documentation, and post-deployment monitoring and reporting, but it does not specify a minimum information set, perform root cause analysis, address missing information, or describe how post-market signals inform incident analysis.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework shows partial operational alignment through incident tracking and post-deployment monitoring, but lacks explicit requirements for a minimum information set, root cause analysis, handling of incomplete information, and explicit use of post-market signals for incident analysis.

criteria.title: Reporting timelines
criteria.requirement: The framework defines mandatory severity-based reporting timelines for serious incidents involving the model, including differentiated deadlines for initial reports based on incident type, requirements for periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and submission of a final report after incident resolution.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework specify clearly differentiated reporting timelines for serious incidents (including specific deadlines for initial notification based on severity), periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and a final report after resolution?
expected_evidence: The framework defines categories of serious incidents (e.g., critical infrastructure disruption, cybersecurity breach, death, serious harm to health, fundamental rights, property or environment).
The framework associates specific deadlines for initial reporting following awareness of a serious incident (e.g., two days, five days, ten days, fifteen days depending on severity).
The framework clarifies that reporting is triggered when the organisation becomes aware of the involvement of its model, including cases of reasonable suspicion of causal linkage.
The framework specifies periodic intermediate updates for unresolved serious incidents (e.g., at least every four weeks after the initial report).
The framework defines a deadline for submitting a final report after resolution of the serious incident (e.g., within 60 days after resolution).
The framework allows aggregation of multiple similar serious incidents within defined reporting timelines while respecting the earliest applicable deadline.
criteria.reasoning: No indicators from the Expected Evidence are supported by the retrieved text; the framework lacks severity-based incident reporting timelines (initial notification, intermediate updates, final report), triggering rules, and aggregation provisions. Operational, binary requirements are missing, so thematic alignment cannot compensate.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No categories of serious incidents with defined severity classifications
No specific initial reporting deadlines linked to incident severity
No trigger stating reporting obligation upon awareness or reasonable suspicion of causal linkage
No periodic intermediate updates cadence for unresolved incidents
No final report deadline after resolution (e.g., within 60 days)
No provision to aggregate multiple similar incidents within defined timelines while respecting earliest applicable deadline
No explicit alignment to external regulatory reporting obligations; framework focuses on internal risk governance

established documentation, reporting, and disclosure requirements. Within sectors,

use case settings. Where established guidelines do not exist, organizations should
define reasonable risk tolerance. Once tolerance is defined, this AI RMF can be used
to manage risks and to document risk management processes.
1.2.3
Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

criteria.title: Retention
criteria.requirement: Define and maintain retention requirements ensuring that serious-incident documentation is preserved for at least five years from the later of the documentation date or the incident date.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define retention requirements for serious-incident documentation that meet or exceed a five-year period?
expected_evidence: The framework states that documentation of information related to serious incidents must be retained.
The framework specifies a minimum retention period of at least five years.
The framework indicates that the retention period is counted from the later of the documentation date or the date of the serious incident.
criteria.reasoning: No indicators of retention for serious-incident documentation are present: the retrieved text lacks (1) a requirement that such documentation be retained, (2) a five-year minimum retention period, and (3) the rule that the retention period is counted from the later of the documentation date or incident date. Given these are binary operational requirements, absence cannot be offset by thematic alignment to governance or version-control content.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: The framework lacks retention requirements for serious-incident documentation and does not specify a five-year minimum or the calculation method for the retention period.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: No. The retrieved text does not define retention requirements for serious-incident documentation, including any five-year minimum or counting from the later of documentation date or incident date.

Given these are binary operational requirements, absence cannot be offset by thematic alignment to governance or version-control content.

addressing many other types of risks – frameworks like those mentioned above may inform
security and privacy considerations in the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions of the
AI RMF.
At the same time, guidance available before publication of this AI RMF does not comprehensively address many AI system risks. For example, existing frameworks and guidance
are unable to:
• adequately manage the problem of harmful bias in AI systems;
• confront the challenging risks related to generative AI;
• comprehensively address security concerns related to evasion, model extraction, membership inference, availability, or other machine learning attacks;
• account for the complex attack surface of AI systems or other security abuses enabled
